content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a work masked motion modeling for self-supervised video representation learning, which substitutes the reconstruction target of VideoMAE from raw rgb pixel to the trajectory motion target. The new target is composed of a position feature and a shape feature, which are concatenated dense trajectory and trajectory-aligned HOG feature. In addition, this paper proposes  trajectory interpolation to further improve the performance. Experimental results demonstrate this paper outperforms previous methods in Kinetics 400 and Something-Something-V2 datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

This paper is well-written and each ablation study demonstrates the effectiveness of each hyper-parameter and designs. 

Also, extensive experiments show the strong performance in two popular video understanding benchmarks.

Weakness:

For the previous VideoMAE, this paper argued that it failed to learn multi-frame interactions as the model can leverage visible areas to easily reconstruct the masked token. This part is not well supported due to the following reasons: 1. There is no well-proved connection between the ability of learning multi-frame interaction (or dependencies) and the difficulty of VideoMAE tasks. It would be good to show the evidence that the harder the reconstruction task the better the video understanding model will be received from VideoMAE. 2. Given the best masking ratio in VideoMAE is as high as 90%, there will be a large number of masked patches that cannot leverage the visible information. 

Similarly, in Figure 3, harder reconstruction may not equal a better video understanding model.

In the introduction: ‘model with more motion details is critical to distinguish different actions’. This statement is not 100% correct. From the two-stream neural network to video transformers, it has been well explored that the importance of spatial and temporal information in action recognition is case by case, depending on the dataset. In this paper, the kinetics dataset is a spatially heavy dataset while the something-something dataset is a temporally heavy dataset. 

In the abstract: this paper claims to track the moving object using optical flow. However, it seems that this paper uses a random tube masking strategy for picking masked tokens (sec 3.2.1). How to make sure the objects will be included in the masks. 

The target name of the last block in Table 1 is not well aligned with the equation. Is $(z^p,z^s)$ equivalent to the Traj (ours) ? is $z^s$ equivalent to the HOG? as it consists of  the HOG features. 

This paper leverages the hand-crafted feature, which is known to be very expensive to compute. It is important to know how much extra cost is introduced. 

This paper utilizes the tube masking, which masks the same spatial location over the time. In this case, how to deal with the moving object? as the object in the time step t may disappear in the same location of time step t+L. 

When compute the trajectory information, how to deal with the moving background and incorrect optical flow caused by huge movement?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: As is mentioned above, there are a few points that require additional supports. Also there is another VideoMAE paper that needs to be cited: Masked Autoencoders As Spatiotemporal Learners, NIPS 2022. This paper demonstrate better result than this paper by using vanilla version of VideoMAE, reconstructing the raw RGB pixels. (Kinetics-400 dataset, ViT-B architecture).
content.summary_of_the_review:
This paper is motivated from the static appearance target in the previous VideoMAE. However, there are two question that are not well answered. 1. Given the high masking ratio, motion information (if there is any) also naturally existed in the masked content. Why is the proposed motion target better? 2. Whether or not harder masking strategy/reconstruction target is the key to improve the performance in the finetuning ? If so, why not simply generate the target in an adversarial fashion?  
I would vote weakly at this point. Looking forward to see the feedback from authors and other reviewers.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presented a new method for self-supervised video representation learning. Specifically, a masked motion modeling (M3Video) approach was proposed to enforce the model to predict the motion of moving objects in the masked regions. Motion position transitions and shape changes of the objects were used to supervise the model training. The model was also enforced to predict trajectory motion in high temporal resolution from low resolution. Experiments on four benchmark datasets show the effectiveness of the proposed method. The main contribution of this paper is the proposed motion trajectory supervision signal for video representation learning.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**

\+ An ablation study was provided, which might be a contribution to following-up research.

\+ The proposed method performs better than the compared methods on several video datasets.

\+ The writing of this paper is generally good.


**Weaknesses**

\- The proposed idea of predicting the motion (trajectory) of objects within the masked regions is a bit misleading and confusing. If an object is never seen by the model (esp. considering a tube-based masking strategy was used), how can its motion be predicted?

\- The novelty and contributions of the proposed method are limited. The overall idea of predicting masked information is similar to several previous works, as also mentioned by the authors. The idea of predicting the motion or tracking objects is also similar to several prior works  [*1, *2]. The idea of interpolating frames was also derived from an existing work [Xiang et al. 2020].

\- The claim of the proposed method "learns long-term fine-grained motion clues" lacks justification to back it up. It is unclear how and why the proposed method learns "long-term" motion and the same for "fine-grained".

\- Missing evidence to support the claim of "the model is easy to finish this mask-and-predict task by only..." (bottom on page 1) in video representation learning.

\- The statement of "interpolating dense trajectories...without increasing computational costs" (bottom on page 2) is overclaimed. Please justify why the added operation did not lead to any additional computational costs.

\- Missing reference to works [*1, *2] with a similar idea of the proposed method, i.e. predicting the motion or tracking the objects.
Besides, when reviewing the related work about "mask-and-predict", reference to key earlier works (e.g. [*3]) was also missing.
For the "self-supervised video representation learning" related works, there are quite a few prior works missing, e.g. [*4].
Suggest the authors carefully and thoroughly do the literature review.

[*1] Wang, J., et al. "Self-supervised spatio-temporal representation learning for videos by predicting motion and appearance statistics." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2019.

[*2] Wang, Xiaolong, Allan Jabri, and Alexei A. Efros. "Learning correspondence from the cycle-consistency of time." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2019.

[*3] Pathak, Deepak, et al. "Context encoders: Feature learning by inpainting." Proceedings of the IEEE conference on computer vision and pattern recognition. 2016.

[*4] Wei, Donglai, et al. "Learning and using the arrow of time." Proceedings of the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2018.

\- Missing (a)-(d) in Figure 4.

\- Duplicated paragraphs for the "Dataset" and "Model" in the Reproducibility statement.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The clarity and quality of the paper are generally okay. But there are some statements and claims that lack convincing justifications as mentioned in the above Weaknesses section. The novelty of this work is also limited, considering very similar ideas proposed in prior works. The proposed method is a bit difficult to be reproduced based on the provided information, but considering that the authors claim to release the code, this should not be an issue.
content.summary_of_the_review: The motivation of trying to propose a new supervision signal for self-supervised video representation learning with a focus on object motion is interesting. But the key idea was not clearly presented, e.g. why the proposed idea of unseen object motion trajectory prediction makes sense. The technical novelty and contributions are also limited, considering the prior works with similar ideas and the missing reference to key previous works. There are also some unconvincing claims without clear justification. The weaknesses overwhelm the strengths of this paper. Overall, the paper in its current form is not ready for publication.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a new mask-and-predict task for self-supervised video learning. Instead of reconstructing the video pixels, the proposed method asks the model to reconstruct the spatially and temporally dense trajectory motion target from the downsampled and masked video input. The trajectory motion target composes of both the object's position and shape changes. With sparse inputs, the proposed strategy can also learn fine-grained motion details. Experiments on four datasets show that the representation learned from the proposed mask-and-predict task performs well on downstream action recognition tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength：
- The paper is well-written and easy to follow.
- The paper extends the mask-and-predict self-supervised video representation learning from the appearance-related target (e.g., raw pixel or HOG feature) to the motion-related target.
- The proposed method surpasses previous works on the action recognition task over several datasets.


Weaknesses：
- The toy experiment in Sec 3.1 does not make sense to me and also makes me confused. I feel this example is hard to support the claim that masked pixels can be well reconstructed by conditioning on the single frame content. Since the video is static, no matter whether the pixel-error-experiment is a single-frame or multi-frame setting, the input information is the same. It is hard to say whether the information comes from the intra- or inter-frame as every frame is the same. Also, for the same experiments that reconstruct your proposed motion target, does it also based on the static video? If yes, the trajectory should be all zero position changes, then how come the single-frame and multi-frame settings can have such a gap? If not, the experiments are unfair to compare. The Pixel error experiments just contain the same amount of information in single-frame and multi-frame settings, while the Traj. error experiments have different information for single-frame and multi-frame settings.

    * The reconstruction error (pixel) and reconstruction error (traj.) have different y-axes. How to compare the gaps when they correspond to different axes? Figure 3 looks misunderstandable.

    * If you want to show that the pixel can be well reconstructed by conditioning on the single-frame content, you may use the original video and show that using either single-frame or multi-frame setting has similar performance, which means that the temporal information is almost not used although it does exist.

    * I think this toy experiment is trivial. Because using a single frame to reconstruct a trajectory is worse than using multiple frames to reconstruct a trajectory is kind of common sense.


- Lack of ablation study. In Table 1, can you also show the result of (1) Traj. with only position changes and (2) Traj. with only shape changes? It is interesting to know which target is more important.

- Lack of reference. I found that one important paper "Action Recognition with Trajectory-Pooled Deep-Convolutional Descriptors" has not been mentioned. It is one of the first successful trajectory-based deep models for video representation learning. 

- Minor: 
    * I suggest removing section A.1 because it is what exactly (Wang et al., 2018) have done before, shrinking section A.2, and replace with proper references.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: The paper is clear, the reading is fluid, and the method and experiments are well presented.

Quality: The quality is ok.

Novelty: The paper proposes to use a motion-based target instead of the appearance-based target, and use the trajectory-based target to explicitly represent the motion information. The evolution of the idea is similar to the time when people were thinking about how to do supervised action recognition -- from appearance to motion and found trajectory was a good representation. The only difference now is to use it as the mask-and-predict target in the self-supervised setting. I feel the idea is straightforward and the novelty is limited.

Reproducibility: Since most of the components are based on previous works that have source code (e.g., optical flow, generating trajectories, mask-and-predict framework), I think the work can be reproduced.
content.summary_of_the_review: The idea of this paper is straightforward and the performance is good, however, I feel the novelty is limited.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
